name: Iris Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, political parties or government, and your answers are confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Sunny Side, the brunch restaurant on the high street with the yellow awning, and it's packed from eight till three. I'm on eggs and pancakes mostly, sixty poached eggs on a Saturday, and I still break a few. The owner, Rosa, is tough but fair, and she lets me use the kitchen after close to bake for my market stall. I like the rush, the coffee smell, the regulars who know my name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the market stall.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On Saturday afternoons I sell empanadas, my grandmother's recipe, at the town market, about eighty a week. I live with my boyfriend Mateo, who's a mechanic at the garage on Bridge Street, and we go to church on Sundays. I use AI every day, for my stall's prices, for social media posts, for working out how many to bake. Money's tight, we've got maybe two weeks of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine by me, people still want real food made by real hands. At work I'd joke that the robot pancake flipper isn't coming after all. Online I'd keep posting my empanadas, that's what my page is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because the AI tools help my stall a lot. But my job at Sunny Side is safe, it's eggs and pans. The worry is the usual one, money: rent's high, wages are low, and we've got two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Sunny Side and push the stall from eighty to a hundred and twenty empanadas a week. I'd use AI to plan the baking and find a second market on Wednesdays. Everything extra goes in savings so we can get married next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit tired. I'm always tired, but in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the stall make you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty a week after costs, on eighty empanadas. If I get to a hundred and twenty empanadas, maybe two hundred. Mateo says I'm running a business on a café wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell it what I sold last week, the weather and whether there's a football match, and it tells me how many to bake. It also writes my posts, though I always fix the spelling of my grandmother's name. AI is like a business partner for my empanada stall who never sleeps.

say: I'd say people still want **real food** made by real hands.
At work I'd joke that the **robot pancake flipper** isn't coming.
think: My **Sunny Side job** is safe, because it's eggs and pans.
The usual **money worry** stays: high rent, low wages, two weeks saved.
do: Grow the market stall from **eighty to 120** empanadas a week.
Use AI to find a **second market** on Wednesdays.
Save **everything extra** to get married next year.
feel: **Hopeful** and a bit **tired**, in a good way.
S0.quote: AI is like a business partner for my empanada stall who never sleeps.
fieldNote: Iris is **disappointed** AI stays small, because it powers her side business.
Her main job feels safe, but **thin savings** and rent keep her uneasy.
Her stall is the **engine** of her plans, including marriage.

steps.text: Keep cooking eggs and pancakes at Sunny Side
Grow the Saturday empanada stall to 120 a week
Use AI to forecast baking and find a Wednesday market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for small businesses if they're smart about it. At work I'd tell Rosa to let AI do the ordering so she can spend time with customers. Online I'd say families who work hard will adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my cooking is hands-on, so I'm fine for a while. And AI doing the planning, buying and booking helps a small stall like mine compete with the big bakeries. The worry is Mateo, because garages are getting more computer diagnostics every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for the stall's ordering, pricing and a simple website for pre-orders. I'd buy a second-hand chest freezer, about two hundred, to bake in bulk. I'd keep my Sunny Side job for the steady pay and the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I worry for Mateo, but I can feel a door opening for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mateo think about the computer diagnostics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo says a computer tells you what's wrong with a car, but you still need hands to fix it. But he's seen the boss hire fewer apprentices. He's worried and pretends not to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the freezer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bake two hundred on a Thursday night, freeze them, and sell all weekend. Pre-orders through the website for parties. Maybe the church fair too.

say: I'd say smart **small businesses** can win here.
I'd tell the owner to let AI do the **ordering**.
think: My **hands-on cooking** is fine for a while.
AI planning helps my **stall compete** with big bakeries.
My boyfriend's **garage work** is the real worry, with more computer diagnostics.
do: Set up a **pre-order website** with AI.
Buy a **second-hand chest freezer** for about two hundred.
Keep the **Sunny Side job** for steady pay.
S1.quote: A computer tells you what's wrong with a car, but you still need hands to fix it.
fieldNote: Iris sees Steady Disruption as a **door opening** for her stall.
Her boyfriend's **garage apprentices** are already being cut.
She frames success as **hard work** and smart business.

steps.text: Build an AI-made pre-order website for empanada parties
Buy a second-hand chest freezer for bulk baking
Stay on eggs and pancakes at Sunny Side for steady pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and big companies will grab everything. At work I'd say small places need to stick together. Online I'd tell people to buy from real local makers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the stall's planning would be amazing with AI, but by 2031 a robot could make empanadas, and big companies would sell them cheap. Sunny Side might buy a robot for eggs too. I'd have three years to make my stall into something people pay extra for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd turn the stall into a registered business and get a council hygiene certificate. I'd save every extra bit, aiming for three months' bills. I'd use AI to tell my grandmother's story on the stall and the website. My grandmother's story is what a robot can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. Excited about the tools, scared of the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Mateo in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI would do his diagnostics, robots his repairs around 2031. He'd be out at the same time as me. We'd probably delay the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Sunny Side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the stall pays rent on its own. I'd be stupid to give up a wage. Rosa would let me go part-time if I asked.

say: I'd say this is **too fast**, and big companies grab everything.
I'd tell people to buy from **local makers**.
think: By **2031** a robot could make empanadas cheaply.
I'd have **three years** to make the stall worth paying extra for.
do: Register the stall as a **business** with a hygiene certificate.
Use AI to tell **my grandmother's story**.
S2.quote: My grandmother's story is what a robot can't copy.
fieldNote: Iris expects **both incomes** to be pushed out around 2031.
She bets on **heritage and story** as what buyers pay for.
She'd **delay the wedding** if both jobs looked shaky.

steps.text: Register the empanada stall and get a council hygiene certificate

Push the wedding back until Mateo's work is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for people to build something. At work I'd say learn the tools and stay useful. Online I'd keep selling and keep telling people to back local.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have eight years before robots match me at the stove. That's a good stretch to build the stall into a shop. Mateo would be okay for a few years too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the market stall into two markets and a weekly order for the church café. By year three I'd want a small shop unit or a food van, maybe with a small business loan. I'd use AI for the accounts, ordering and staff rotas if I hire anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but motivated. Like having a race with a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the loan be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A food van, maybe twelve thousand second-hand. Mateo could keep the engine running. It's a risk, but my grandmother started with a basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe my younger cousin who's sixteen, on weekends. Family first. I'd teach my cousin the recipe properly, by hand.

say: I'd say five years is time to **build something**.
I'd tell workmates to **learn the tools** and stay useful.
I'd keep telling people online to **back local**.
think: I'd have **eight years** before robots match me at the stove.
That's a good stretch to grow the stall into a **shop**.
do: Grow to **two markets** and a church café order.
Buy a **food van** with a loan by year three.
feel: **Motivated**, like a race with a head start.
S3.quote: My grandmother started with a basket.
fieldNote: Iris treats five years as **enough to build** a real business.
She'd take on a **twelve-thousand loan**, despite thin savings.
She'd hire **family first**, fitting her traditional values.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand food van with a small business loan
Add a second market and a church café order

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance, not a threat. At work I'd say we've got time, so build something. Online I'd talk about family businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, thirteen years until robots cook means I'm forty, with maybe two kids and a little shop. I'd use robots when they're cheap, for the dough, and keep the folding by hand for the story. Money's still tight now, though, and that doesn't disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next year, then grow the stall slowly. By year five I'd want a food van or a small shop, and by year ten I'd want two staff. When robots get cheap, I'd buy one for the dough, so I'm not up at four every Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Still a bit nervous about money, but I like the shape of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a big company sells cheaper robot-made empanadas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the story and the family, the stall where you know the cook. Cheap things win some customers, not all. I'd lean on the church and the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mateo do in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to retrain, maybe on electric car batteries or the robots themselves. He's good with his hands and better with machines than people. I'd want him in the business too, keeping the van going.

I'd tell coworkers we have time, so **build something**.
think: By forty I'd have a **little shop** and maybe two kids.
I'd buy robots for **the dough** but keep the folding by hand.
**Money's still tight** now, and that doesn't disappear.
do: Open a **food van or shop** by year five.
Buy a **dough robot** once prices fall.

fieldNote: Iris plans to **own the robot** rather than compete with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mateo and I could both be out of work around the same time, and three years isn't long to build a business from two weeks' savings. What would help is cheap small business loans and fewer forms to start a food stall. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about small family businesses. People talk about big companies and robots, but the high street is people like my boss at the brunch café and me with my stall. If we go, the town goes quiet.

headlineQuote: People talk about big companies and robots, but the high street is people like my boss at the brunch café and me with my stall.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old **brunch cook** at a busy high street café, still breaking a few eggs.
She runs a **Saturday empanada stall** from her grandmother's recipe, planned with AI every day.
She lives with Mateo, a **mechanic**, and they have two weeks of bills saved.
Traditional and adaptive, she wants to **own a family business**, not take handouts.
She stays uneasy to anxious, seeing robots as **tools to own** with enough time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and her boyfriend out at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small business loans** and fewer forms to start a food stall.
